title: Which response is this?
lede: A family member says each of these to you on placement. Real people often show more than one response at once, so pick the one each shows most clearly.
intent: Learners can recognise each of the five responses from what a family member actually says.
goal: recognise each of the five responses from what a family member actually says.
prompt: Which response does each of these show most clearly?

categories.label: Anger
categories.hint: Blame, often aimed at whoever is in the room.

categories.label: Bargaining
categories.hint: If I do this, then that. Or if only.

items.text: "The scan must have been someone else's. These things get mixed up all the time."
items.why: It rejects the information itself. The cue is disbelief about the facts, rather than distress about them.

items.text: "Why did it take three months for anyone to send him for a scan?"
items.why: The blame points outward, at the system. It accepts the diagnosis and is furious about how it arrived.

items.text: "If I get him walking every day and off the sugar, that will buy him more time, won't it?"
items.why: A deal: if I do this, then that. It sounds practical and hopeful, which is exactly why it is easy to miss.

items.text: "I don't see the point in getting dressed any more."
items.why: Loss of meaning in ordinary things. Listen, and pass it on to your supervisor. This is where you watch for risk.

items.text: "I want to sit down with the kids this weekend and talk about what he would want."
items.why: Planning around the reality rather than against it. Acceptance is not happiness. It is engaging with what is.

items.text: "You people are useless. Nobody tells us anything."
items.why: Aimed at the person in the room. It is almost never about that person, so it is worth not taking it personally.

items.text: "I keep thinking if I had made him go to the doctor sooner, none of this would be happening."
items.why: "If only" looks backwards, but it is the same move as a deal: searching for the lever that would have changed the outcome. It often comes with guilt.

items.text: "He's fine. He was up and about this morning. He just needs a good rest."
items.why: The evidence of the morning is used to push away the diagnosis. Denial often protects someone while the news sinks in.

items.text: "I haven't been sleeping. I just sit in his room."
items.why: Withdrawal, and a sign of how much this is costing them. Worth mentioning to the team so someone checks on the family as well as the resident.

teach.watchFor: Learners who treat the sort as a diagnosis. It is practice in noticing, not in labelling people. On placement, nobody should be told which stage they are in.
ask: Which two were hardest to tell apart? What was the cue that settled it?
Bargaining sounds hopeful. Why might that make it easy to miss?

sources.label: Client statements written for this activity
sources.note: Check with a practitioner that each reads as realistic for an aged care or palliative setting.

sources.label: Kübler-Ross, E. (1969). On Death and Dying.
sources.note: Check the descriptions of each response against the unit's prescribed reading.
